summary.text: A finite sine–cotangent Fourier identity expresses the sum of the centered quadratic residues as a negative multiple of an associated value at \(s=1\), while quadratic Gauss-sum evaluations and a gcd decomposition reduce its nonnegativity to positivity of real Dirichlet-character \(L\)-series via their Euler products. Thus the centered sum is nonpositive, giving the stronger bound \(a(n)\le n(n-1)/2\), which immediately implies the claimed inequality.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(k^2\bmod n).
\]
This is the same as the sum from \(k=1\) to \(n\), because the terms at \(k=0\) and \(k=n\) are both zero. We shall prove the stronger estimate
\[
a(n)\leq \frac{n(n-1)}2. \tag{1}
\]
Here and below, an inequality containing halves is first understood over the real numbers; at the end we return to integer division.

The main point is a sign inequality for a sawtooth sum. Its proof uses quadratic Gauss sums and positivity of Dirichlet series. We develop all the ingredients in turn.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Quadratic Gauss sums for an odd modulus
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For positive integers \(N,m\), put
\[
e_N(a)=\exp(2\pi i a/N),\qquad
G_N(m)=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}e_N(mk^2).
\]
We first need the exact evaluation of \(G_N(m)\) when \(N\) is odd and \((m,N)=1\).

For a unit \(u\pmod N\), let \(\sigma_N(u)\in\{1,-1\}\) be the sign of the permutation
\[
x\longmapsto ux
\]
of \(\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\). We claim that for odd \(N\),
\[
G_N(u)=\sigma_N(u)\,\varepsilon_N\sqrt N,
\qquad
\varepsilon_N=
\begin{cases}
1,&N\equiv1\pmod4,\\
i,&N\equiv3\pmod4.
\end{cases} \tag{2}
\]
We give Schur's matrix proof, including the sign determination.

Write \(\psi(x)=e^{2\pi i x/N}\) for the standard additive character of \(\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\), and form the \(N\times N\) matrix
\[
A_u=(\psi(ujk))_{j,k\bmod N}.
\]
Also let \(P\) be the permutation matrix for negation, so that \(P_{jk}=1\) exactly when \(j+k=0\). Orthogonality of additive characters gives
\[
A_u^2=NP. \tag{3}
\]
Indeed, its \((j,k)\)-entry is
\[
\sum_{\ell\bmod N}\psi(uj\ell)\psi(u\ell k)
 =\sum_{\ell\bmod N}\psi\bigl(\ell u(j+k)\bigr),
\]
which is \(N\) if \(j+k=0\), and zero otherwise. Since \(P^2=I\), it follows that
\[
A_u^4=N^2I. \tag{4}
\]
The trace is the Gauss sum:
\[
\operatorname{tr}(A_u)=\sum_j\psi(uj^2)=G_N(u). \tag{5}
\]
Because \(N\) is odd, negation has exactly one fixed point, namely zero. Thus \(\operatorname{tr}P=1\), and (3) gives
\[
\operatorname{tr}(A_u^2)=N. \tag{6}
\]
A second use of character orthogonality gives the absolute-value formula
\[
|G_N(u)|^2=N. \tag{7}
\]
For completeness, after conjugating the second sum one has
\[
|G_N(u)|^2=\sum_{j,k}\psi(u(j^2-k^2)).
\]
Replace \(j\) by \(j+k\). Then
\[
u((j+k)^2-k^2)=uj^2+2ujk.
\]
On summing first over \(k\), the inner character sum is zero unless \(2uj=0\). Since both \(2\) and \(u\) are units modulo the odd number \(N\), only \(j=0\) survives, yielding \(N\).

It remains to determine the phase. First consider \(A_1\). It is a Vandermonde matrix on the roots \(1,\zeta,\ldots,\zeta^{N-1}\), where \(\zeta=e^{2\pi i/N}\), and hence
\[
\det A_1=\prod_{0\le i<j<N}(\zeta^j-\zeta^i). \tag{8}
\]
For \(i<j\),
\[
\zeta^j-\zeta^i
=e^{\pi i(i+j)/N}\,2i\sin\frac{\pi(j-i)}N. \tag{9}
\]
Every sine on the right is positive. There are \(N(N-1)/2\) factors. Furthermore,
\[
\sum_{0\le i<j<N}(i+j)
=(N-1)\sum_{r=0}^{N-1}r
=(N-1)\frac{N(N-1)}2.
\]
If \(N=2h+1\), this last integer is \(N\cdot 2h^2\), so the product of the exponential factors in (9) is
\(e^{2\pi i h^2}=1\). Consequently
\[
\det A_1=i^{N(N-1)/2}R \tag{10}
\]
for some positive real number \(R\). Multiplication of the row index by \(u\) changes \(A_1\) into \(A_u\), and therefore
\[
\det A_u=\sigma_N(u)\det A_1. \tag{11}
\]

By (4), every eigenvalue of \(A_u\) is one of
\[
s,\ -s,\ is,\ -is,\qquad s=\sqrt N.
\]
Let their multiplicities be \(a,b,c,d\), respectively. Characteristic polynomials split over \(\mathbb C\), and the trace of a square is the sum of the squares of the eigenvalues, so (5)--(7), (6), and (10)--(11) imply
\[
\begin{aligned}
a+b+c+d&=2h+1,\\
a+b-c-d&=1,\\
(a-b)^2+(c-d)^2&=1, \tag{12}\\
i^{2b+c+3d}&=\sigma_N(u)i^{(2h+1)h}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The third line follows by writing
\(G_N(u)=s((a-b)+i(c-d))\) and using \(|G_N(u)|^2=N=s^2\). The last line is the equality of determinant phases; equality of absolute values removes the positive factor \(R\).

The integer solutions of \(X^2+Y^2=1\) are
\((\pm1,0)\) and \((0,\pm1)\). Substituting these four possibilities into the other equations in (12), and reducing the last equation modulo the period four of powers of \(i\), gives:
\[
\begin{cases}
c=d,\ a-b=\sigma_N(u),&h\text{ even},\\
a=b,\ c-d=\sigma_N(u),&h\text{ odd}.
\end{cases} \tag{13}
\]
This is a four-case calculation for \((a-b,c-d)\), followed in each case by the two possible values of \(\sigma_N(u)\) and the four residues of \(h\pmod4\). Equivalently, the determinant phase rules out the sign opposite to that displayed in (13). Since \(N=2h+1\) is \(1\pmod4\) precisely when \(h\) is even, equations (5) and (13) prove (2).

We will regard \(m\mapsto\sigma_N(m)\), extended by zero on nonunits, as a real-valued Dirichlet character modulo odd \(N\). Denote it by \(S_N\). Thus (2) reads
\[
G_N(m)=S_N(m)\varepsilon_N\sqrt N\qquad ((m,N)=1). \tag{14}
\]

We also need the value of \(S_N(2)\). Zolotarev's sign count gives
\[
S_N(2)=\chi_8(N), \tag{15}
\]
where, for odd \(r\),
\[
\chi_8(r)=
\begin{cases}
1,&r\equiv1,7\pmod8,\\
-1,&r\equiv3,5\pmod8.
\end{cases}
\]
Here is the required count. Write \(N=2h+1\). In the ordered list \(0,1,\ldots,N-1\), the number of earlier entries \(i<j\) for which
\((2i\bmod N)>(2j\bmod N)\) is, for fixed \(j\),
\[
\begin{cases}
N-j,&j>h,\\
0,&j\le h.
\end{cases}
\]
Indeed, \(2x\bmod N\) is \(2x\) for \(x\le h\), and \(2x-N\) for \(x>h\). Hence the sign is
\[
(-1)^C,
\qquad C=\sum_{j=h+1}^{2h}(2h+1-j)=\frac{h(h+1)}2.
\]
Checking \(h=0,1,2,3\pmod4\) shows that \((-1)^C\) has exactly the values \(\chi_8(2h+1)\), proving (15).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. The imaginary part of a general Gauss sum
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We next prove the structural fact needed for positivity.

**Gauss-sum structure lemma.** For every \(N>0\), there are a constant \(c_N\ge0\) and a real-valued Dirichlet character \(\chi_N\) modulo \(N\), with \(|\chi_N(a)|\le1\), such that
\[
\operatorname{Im}G_N(m)=c_N\chi_N(m) \tag{16}
\]
whenever \((m,N)=1\).

We prove this by separating the power of two in \(N\). We use the Chinese remainder identity
\[
G_{N_1N_2}(m)=G_{N_1}(mN_2)G_{N_2}(mN_1)
\quad\text{if }(N_1,N_2)=1. \tag{17}
\]
To see this, parametrize residues modulo \(N_1N_2\) by
\[
k=N_2x+N_1y\pmod{N_1N_2},
\quad 0\le x<N_1,
\quad 0\le y<N_2.
\]
Coprimality makes this parametrization bijective. Expanding the square, the cross term is a multiple of \(N_1N_2\), and the two remaining exponentials give the two factors in (17).

We also use the elementary evaluations
\[
\begin{aligned}
G_2(m)&=1+(-1)^m,\\
G_4(m)&=2(1+i^m),\\
G_8(m)&=2+4e_8(m)+2(-1)^m. \tag{18}
\end{aligned}
\]
They follow simply by listing the squares modulo \(2,4,8\). For odd \(m\),
\[
e_8(m)=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\bigl(\chi_8(m)+i\chi'_8(m)\bigr), \tag{19}
\]
where
\[
\chi'_8(m)=
\begin{cases}
1,&m\equiv1,3\pmod8,\\
-1,&m\equiv5,7\pmod8.
\end{cases}
\]
Also, if \(m\) is odd, \(i^m=i\chi_4(m)\), with \(\chi_4(m)=1\) for \(m\equiv1\pmod4\) and \(-1\) for \(m\equiv3\pmod4\).

Write \(N=2^kt\), with \(t\) odd. Formulae (14), (17)--(19), and (15) give the following choices (characters originally modulo \(t,4,8\) are lifted to modulus \(N\)):

* If \(k=0\), take \(c_N=0\) when \(t\equiv1\pmod4\), and take \(c_N=\sqrt t\), \(\chi_N=S_t\), when \(t\equiv3\pmod4\).

* If \(k=1\), then for \((m,N)=1\), both \(m\) and \(t\) are odd and the factor \(G_2(mt)=1+(-1)^{mt}\) is zero. Thus take \(c_N=0\) and the trivial character.

* If \(k=2\), take \(c_N=2\sqrt t\). If \(t\equiv1\pmod4\), take
\(\chi_N=S_t\chi_4\); if \(t\equiv3\pmod4\), take \(\chi_N=S_t\).

* If \(k=3\), take \(c_N=2\sqrt2\sqrt t\). If \(t\equiv1\pmod4\), take
\(\chi_N=S_t\chi'_8\); if \(t\equiv3\pmod4\), take
\(\chi_N=S_t\chi_8\).

For example, these assertions follow by inserting (14) into (17), then using (18)--(19). The factor introduced by multiplying the odd argument of \(S_t\) by \(4\) is \(S_t(4)=S_t(2)^2=1\), while multiplication by \(8\) introduces \(S_t(8)=S_t(2)=\chi_8(t)\); these are exactly the signs absorbed in the characters displayed above. Every listed character is real and has absolute value at most one.

It remains to handle \(k\ge4\). For odd \(m\) one has
\[
G_{16L}(m)=2G_{4L}(m). \tag{20}
\]
To verify this, split the defining sum into even and odd indices. The even-indexed terms form twice the sum defining \(G_{4L}(m)\), because the summand has period \(4L\). The odd-indexed terms cancel: shifting the half-index by \(2L\) multiplies the corresponding exponential by \((-1)^m=-1\), and a further shift by \(2L\) restores it. Thus the odd terms occur in opposite pairs. Applying the structure lemma inductively to \(4L<N=16L\), then lifting its character to modulus \(16L\), proves (16), with the constant doubled. This completes the proof of the structure lemma.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Positivity of the Dirichlet series formed from \(\operatorname{Im}G_N(m)\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Define the periodic real-valued function
\[
\Phi_N(m)=\operatorname{Im}G_N(m).
\]
For real \(s>1\), consider
\[
L(\Phi_N,s)=\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\frac{\Phi_N(m)}{m^s}. \tag{21}
\]
The series converges absolutely, since \(|G_N(m)|\le N\) by the triangle inequality.

We claim
\[
L(\Phi_N,s)\ge0\qquad(s>1). \tag{22}
\]
The structure lemma applies only to arguments coprime to the modulus, so we decompose according to the gcd. For each divisor \(d\mid N\), let
\[
\Phi_{N,d}(m)=
\begin{cases}
\Phi_N(m),&\gcd(m,N)=d,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Then \(\Phi_N=\sum_{d\mid N}\Phi_{N,d}\).

Write \(N=dN'\). The terms supported on gcd \(d\) have \(m=dm'\) with \((m',N')=1\). Directly from the exponential sum,
\[
G_{dN'}(dm')=dG_{N'}(m'). \tag{23}
\]
Indeed, each summand reduces to \(e_{N'}(m'k^2)\), and as \(k\) runs modulo \(dN'\), every residue modulo \(N'\) occurs exactly \(d\) times. By (16), for a suitable \(c\ge0\) and real character \(\chi\) modulo \(N'\),
\[
\Phi_{N,d}(dm')=dc\chi(m')
\]
when \((m',N')=1\), while both sides are zero when \(m'\) is not a unit. Consequently
\[
L(\Phi_{N,d},s)=d^{1-s}cL(\chi,s). \tag{24}
\]

For every real-valued Dirichlet character \(\chi\) with \(|\chi|\le1\), its Euler product shows that
\[
L(\chi,s)>0\qquad(s>1). \tag{25}
\]
Indeed,
\[
L(\chi,s)=\prod_p(1-\chi(p)p^{-s})^{-1}
 =\exp\left(-\sum_p\log(1-\chi(p)p^{-s})\right).
\]
Since \(|\chi(p)|\le1\) and \(p^{-s}<1\), every number
\(1-\chi(p)p^{-s}\) is a positive real number. Thus the sum in the exponential is real and the exponential is strictly positive. Equations (24)--(25), with \(d^{1-s}c\ge0\), show that every gcd-piece has a nonnegative \(L\)-series. Summing over the finitely many divisors of \(N\) proves (22).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Passage to \(s=1\) and the cotangent formula
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We now express the limiting value at \(s=1\) as a finite cotangent sum.

Regard
\[
\Phi'_N(j)=\sum_{k\bmod N}\operatorname{Im}\psi(jk^2),
\qquad j\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z.
\]
For an integer \(m\), this equals \(\Phi_N(m)\). Complex conjugation of \(\psi(jk^2)\) gives
\[
\Phi'_N(-j)=-\Phi'_N(j), \tag{26}
\]
so \(\Phi'_N\) is odd. In particular,
\[
\sum_{j\bmod N}\Phi'_N(j)=0. \tag{27}
\]

For an odd periodic function \(f\) of period \(N\), its analytically continued periodic \(L\)-function can be written as
\[
\mathcal L(f,s)=N^{-s}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}f(j)\,H_{\rm odd}(j/N,s), \tag{28}
\]
where \(H_{\rm odd}(a,s)\) is the odd part of the Hurwitz zeta function. For real \(s>1\), (28) agrees with the ordinary Dirichlet series \(\sum_{m\ge1}f(m)m^{-s}\). Because of the zero-sum relation (27), it is continuous at \(s=1\).

We require the value
\[
H_{\rm odd}(a,1)=\frac\pi2\cot(\pi a),
\qquad 0<a<1. \tag{29}
\]
Here is a derivation that also justifies the limiting process. For \(s>1\), pair positive and negative integers in the odd Hurwitz series to obtain
\[
H_{\rm odd}(a,s)
 =\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}F(a,s,r),
\quad
F(a,s,r)=\frac{(r+a)^{-s}-(r+1-a)^{-s}}2. \tag{30}
\]
For \(1\le s\le2\), the mean-value (or Bernoulli) estimate for \(x\mapsto x^{-s}\) gives, with \(\delta=\min(a,1-a)>0\),
\[
|F(a,s,r)|\le \delta^{-3}(r+1)^{-2}. \tag{31}
\]
One way to see (31) is to use
\[
|u^{-s}-v^{-s}|
 \le s|v-u|\min(u,v)^{-s-1},
\]
then note that \(|(r+1-a)-(r+a)|=|1-2a|\le1\) and
\(\min(r+a,r+1-a)\ge\delta(r+1)\). The right side of (31) is summable, so dominated convergence allows \(s\downarrow1\) term by term.

At \(s=1\), the classical partial-fraction expansion of cotangent gives
\[
\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}
\left(\frac1{r+a}-\frac1{r+1-a}\right)
=\pi\cot(\pi a). \tag{32}
\]
For completeness, (32) follows from
\[
\pi\cot(\pi a)=\frac1a+
\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}
\left(\frac1{a-(r+1)}+\frac1{a+(r+1)}\right),
\]
and the telescoping identity
\[
\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}
\left(\frac1{r+a}-\frac1{r+1+a}\right)=\frac1a.
\]
Combining these two series and simplifying each term yields (32). Equations (30)--(32) prove (29).

Applying (28)--(29) to \(f=\Phi'_N\), noting that the term \(j=0\) vanishes, gives
\[
\mathcal L(\Phi'_N,1)
=\frac{\pi}{2N}\sum_{m=0}^{N-1}
\Phi_N(m)\cot\frac{\pi m}{N}. \tag{33}
\]
For \(s>1\), this \(L\)-function is \(L(\Phi_N,s)\), which is nonnegative by (22). Continuity at \(s=1\), and closedness of the nonnegative real axis, therefore imply
\[
\mathcal L(\Phi'_N,1)\ge0.
\]
Since \(\pi/(2N)>0\), (33) yields the crucial cotangent inequality
\[
\sum_{m=0}^{N-1}
\operatorname{Im}G_N(m)\cot\frac{\pi m}{N}\ge0. \tag{34}
\]
The apparently singular \(m=0\) term is interpreted through (33); it is zero because \(\Phi_N(0)=0\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. A finite sine--cotangent identity
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For integers \(0<x<N\), we claim
\[
\sum_{m=0}^{N-1}
\sin\frac{2\pi mx}{N}\cot\frac{\pi m}{N}=N-2x. \tag{35}
\]
The \(m=0\) term is zero. For \(1\le m<N\), put \(\varphi=\pi m/N\). Since \(0<\varphi<\pi\), \(\sin\varphi\ne0\), and the elementary identity
\[
\sin(2x\varphi)\cos\varphi
=\sin\varphi\left(2\sum_{j=0}^{x-1}\cos(2j\varphi)-1+
\cos(2x\varphi)\right) \tag{36}
\]
gives, after division by \(\sin\varphi\),
\[
\sin(2x\varphi)\cot\varphi
=2\sum_{j=0}^{x-1}\cos(2j\varphi)-1+
\cos(2x\varphi). \tag{37}
\]
Identity (36) follows by induction on \(x\) from the addition formulae for sine and cosine.

Now sum (37) over \(m=1,\ldots,N-1\). For \(0<j<N\), the geometric-series identity for the nontrivial \(N\)-th root \(e^{2\pi i j/N}\) gives
\[
\sum_{m=0}^{N-1}\cos\frac{2\pi jm}{N}=0,
\]
so the sum over \(m=1,\ldots,N-1\) is \(-1\). For \(j=0\), that sum is \(N-1\). In (37), the \(j=0\) term therefore contributes \(2(N-1)\); the other \(x-1\) inner cosine sums contribute \(-2(x-1)\); the constant \(-1\) contributes \(-(N-1)\); and the last cosine contributes \(-1\). Their total is
\[
2(N-1)-2(x-1)-(N-1)-1=N-2x,
\]
which proves (35).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. The sawtooth inequality
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Define the centered sawtooth
\[
((y))_N=
\begin{cases}
0,&N\mid y,\\
\dfrac{y\bmod N}{N}-\dfrac12,&N\nmid y.
\end{cases} \tag{38}
\]
We claim that for every positive \(N\),
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}((k^2))_N\le0. \tag{39}
\]

Fix \(k\), and put \(x=k^2\bmod N\). The sine in (35) is unchanged if \(k^2\) is replaced by \(x\). If \(x=0\), every sine vanishes and both sides of the following identity are zero. If \(0<x<N\), (35) says
\[
((k^2))_N=\frac{x}{N}-\frac12
=-\frac1{2N}\sum_{m=0}^{N-1}
\sin\frac{2\pi m k^2}{N}\cot\frac{\pi m}{N}. \tag{40}
\]
Thus (40) holds in all cases.

Sum (40) over \(k\), interchange the two finite sums, and use
\[
\operatorname{Im}G_N(m)
=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\sin\frac{2\pi m k^2}{N}.
\]
We obtain
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}((k^2))_N
=-\frac1{2N}\sum_{m=0}^{N-1}
\operatorname{Im}G_N(m)\cot\frac{\pi m}{N}.
\]
The sum on the right after the minus sign is nonnegative by (34), and \(1/(2N)>0\). This proves (39).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Conversion back to quadratic residues
--------------------------------------------------------------------

From the definition (38), for every \(k\),
\[
k^2\bmod N
=N((k^2))_N+
\begin{cases}
0,&N\mid k^2,\\
N/2,&N\nmid k^2.
\end{cases} \tag{41}
\]
This is an identity of real numbers. Summing (41) for \(0\le k<N\), the first part is nonpositive by (39). In the second part, the \(k=0\) term is zero, and each of the other \(N-1\) terms is at most \(N/2\). Therefore
\[
a(N)=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(k^2\bmod N)
\le N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}((k^2))_N+(N-1)\frac N2
\le\frac{N(N-1)}2.
\]
This proves the stronger real inequality (1).

Because \(a(N)\) and \(N(N-1)\) are integers, (1) implies
\[
2a(N)\le N(N-1),
\]
and hence, with ordinary integer division,
\[
a(N)\le \left\lfloor\frac{N(N-1)}2\right\rfloor.
\tag{42}
\]

Finally, for \(N\ge1\),
\[
N(N-1)\le N^2-1,
\]
since the difference is \(N-1\ge0\). Integer division by the positive integer \(2\) preserves order, so (42) gives
\[
a(N)\le \left\lfloor\frac{N^2-1}{2}\right\rfloor.
\]
As \(N^2-1\) is in fact always even or, more simply, as the displayed expression is exactly the natural-number quotient appearing in the conjecture, this is the desired result for every integer \(N\ge1\).
